evidence: src/delivery/__models__/deliveryman.model.ts: @Entity('deliverymans') class Deliveryman with @OneToMany(() => Order, order => order.deliveryman). The order-count rule (addOrder) and the deactivation rule (changeStatus) live only here.

src/delivery/__models__/orders.model.ts: @Entity('orders') class Order with @ManyToOne(() => Deliveryman, ...). The name check (checkName, called from create) and the state changes (deliver/return/addInfoToDescription) live only here.
Deliveryman.addNewMessageToOrders calls order.addInfoToDescription(...) instead of setting order.description directly, so it uses Order's own method.
Neither file copies the other's rules. The two changeStatus methods enforce different rules for each entity.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
Both files define the two TypeORM entities of one concern: the delivery aggregate of a Deliveryman and its Orders. They are linked as two sides of one relationship (@OneToMany / @ManyToOne). Each class keeps its own rules in one place:
- Order keeps the name-length check (checkName) and its delivery-state changes (deliver, return, addInfoToDescription).
- Deliveryman keeps the order-count limit (addOrder) and the rule that a deliveryman can't be deactivated while holding orders (changeStatus).

No rule is copied between the two files. When Deliveryman changes an order's description, it calls Order.addInfoToDescription rather than writing to order.description directly, so it uses the module's own method. The two changeStatus methods share a name but enforce different rules. Possible bugs (Order.return never sets isActive back to true; addOrder's '> 3' check allows a fourth order) are about correctness, not cohesion, so they don't fail this rule.
